Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

dare verb

also daren’t, dared, venture, would dare

classical

Verg. A. 6.14–15: Daedalus … ausus sē crēdere caelō
Hor. Ep. 1.2.40: sapere audē

audeō, audēre, ausus sum

verb, second conjugation, semi-deponent, with an infinitive

dare, venture

The perfect is passive in form: ausus sum, I dared. The old subjunctive ausim, “I would dare”, is found in comedy, in the poets, and in Livy’s preface (Lewis & Short). Cicero explains sōdēs, “please”, as sī audēs, “if you will” (Or. 154, cited by Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • dīmidium factī, quī coepit, habet; sapere audē, incipe

    well begun is half done: dare to be wise, make a startHor. Ep. 1.2.40–41

  • Daedalus, ut fāma est, … praepetibus pennīs ausus sē crēdere caelō

    Daedalus, so the story goes, … dared to trust himself to the sky on swift wingsVerg. A. 6.14–15

  • sōlem quis dīcere falsum audeat?

    Who would dare to call the sun a liar?Verg. G. 1.463–464

  • nec satis sciō nec, sī sciam, dīcere ausim

    I don’t really know, and if I did, I wouldn’t dare sayLiv. praef. 1

  • nōn ausim quicquam dēpōnere tēcum

    I wouldn’t dare bet anything against youVerg. Ecl. 3.32

  • quid dulcius quam habēre quīcum omnia audeās sīc loquī ut tēcum?

    what is sweeter than having someone you dare speak to about everything as if to yourself?Cic. Amic. 22

See also would, able.

SourcesLewis & Short: audeo · Lewis & Short: sodes
